Thanks!

Martín

On Thu, Feb 16, 2017 at 11:28 AM, Nick Matzke <nick....@anu.edu.au> wrote:
> We did something like this for:
>
> Dupin, Julia; Matzke, Nicholas J.; Sarkinen, Tiina; Knapp, Sandra; Olmstead, Richard; Bohs, Lynn; Smith, Stacey (2015). Bayesian estimation of the global biogeographic history of the Solanaceae. Journal of Biogeography, accepted September 4, 2016.
> http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jbi.12898/abstract
> http://datadryad.org/resource/doi:10.5061/dryad.6gd57
>
> Short version:
>
> 1. Run Biogeographical Stochastic Mapping (BSM) with the (PhyloWiki version of) BioGeoBEARS. This produces tables of the times and type of biogeographical events, including which sections of which branches have which geographic ranges for a particular single BSM.
>
> 2. Use an R script to count how many lineages are in each area at each time-point of interest (use 10 or 100 time points or whatever) for a single stochastic map
>
> 3. Average over, say, 100 stochastic maps
>
> You could probably get the code for #2-#3 from Julia Dupin, or perhaps it's in that Dryad link, I forget.  I don't think the code is particularly "ready to use", so it might be easier to script it yourself.
>
> If this is all sounds overwhelmingly complex then it may be something you need to find a collaborator to do, it would take more time to explain it in detail than it would be to just do it I think...
>
> Cheers!
> Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi all -- it's possible this is due to something having changed in the R backend about how classes are set up, such that however I set up the "tipranges" class is now invalid. But if that were true generally I would expect everyone to be getting this error.

I am travelling at the moment, but if someone getting this error wants to make progress before I find a way to replicate the issue, the basic procedure would be:

type getranges_from_LagrangePHYLIP, and hit return. This will display that function's code to the screen.

Copy-and-paste that function's code into a .R file.

Run through that code line-by-line until you get the error. Repeat the get-the-code trick if it's another BioGeoBEARS function inside that is causing the error.

Sometimes, the solution will be obvious just from that, or at least the problem will be more obvious. Either way, report back!

Cheers, Nick

messages.body_plain:
Interesting quick discussion...

---------- Forwarded message ----------
From:  <erik...@gmail.com>
Date: Wed, Feb 22, 2017 at 11:24 AM
Subject: Re: Question about large trees in BioGeoBEARS
To: Nick Matzke <mat...@nimbios.org>

Hi Nick,
Thanks so much for this rapid and thorough response! I really appreciate it. I think these simple options all get at the point very well. The incorporation of time stratification and changing matrices is an awesome feature to incorporate heterogeneity. As you mentioned in the first option, my question is essentially solved by simply dividing up the tree so the model is allowed to vary across clades. This is how I have been going about some preliminary analyses of my own, but was curious your take given a few recently published “very large” analyses. Even if the differences are minimal, it seems like it would be important to check. Thanks again for your response, and yes please feel free to post this to the google group!

Thanks!

Hi!  I think it's quite likely that biogeographical and diversification processes might be heterogenous across large trees, as you say.  However, dealing with it is not so simple!  In the first place, all but the simplest of the biogeographical models currently available make weird implicit assumptions -- like they assume no extinction, so a "totally realistic" model would have to solve that issue. (It is solved in SSE models, but these seem to have severe computational limitations.)  In the second place, available models are clearly pretty crude, so it's debatable if taking those crude models and then implementing e.g. a model-transitioning apparatus to allow the crude model to change at different points on the tree would be worth it.

There are some simpler options that would allow us to make progress:

- one could always just divide up a tree and run BioGeoBEARS separately on each chunk of interest.

- if the idea is that the rates changed by time-slice or by geographic region, these can be addressed with time-stratification, changing distance matrices, etc.

- if the idea is that rates changed by an evolving trait, I now have the trait-based dispersal model in BioGeoBEARS, although I haven't had time to write a tutorial or whatever, I am collaborating with a few interested people.

My philosophy is the Burnham and Anderson (2002) philosophy, which is basically we can make progress by comparing a relatively few fairly simple models, looking for main effects that the old models missed.  Once we get a sense that a particular effect is commonly important, we can work to include it in models in a more routine way...

Cheers!
Nick

PS Can I post this to the BioGeoBEARS google group to help others?

On Wed, Feb 22, 2017 at 7:56 AM, <erik...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Nick,
> My name is Erik Funk and I’m currently a graduate student at San Diego State University. I’ve recently enjoyed running quite a few analyses using BioGeoBEARS and was wondering if I could get your opinion on a question relating to large trees.
>
> I’ve looked through the forum a bit, and most people seem to be interested in how small a tree can be to retain significance, or how large for computation purposes. Recently I’ve seen a few studies estimate biogeographic range on extremely large trees (100’s of species). What I am wondering is how disparity in diversification rate and range evolution across different clades within the tree might affect parameter estimation and model selection. To clarify a bit, I imagine its possible, given a large enough tree, to have two clades that differ significantly in the way they have evolved biogeographically. Thus, if run separately they might vary greatly in their parameters or even best fit model (perhaps especially if trying to incorporate distance?). I am wondering if you have (or if you know of anyone who has) any insight to this question, and what these effects might be. Any input you have on this subject is much appreciated!
>
> Best,
> Erik
>
